33-6.title: Do not buy a therapy or device that claims to cure paralysis, blindness or deafness
33-6.inPlainWords: No therapy or device has been proven to cure a complete spinal-cord injury, a mature cataract or a sensorineural hearing loss. A claim to 'cure' paralysis, blindness or deafness is a red flag. The Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016 and the Consumer Protection Act, 2019 give you a remedy, and the medical council can act on a false claim. Ask for the evidence, not a testimonial.
33-6.benefit: The RPwD Act, 2016 protects the rights of a person with a disability and prohibits discrimination. The Consumer Protection Act, 2019 covers a misleading advertisement and a deficient service. The National Medical Commission and the state medical council can act on a false claim by a doctor. A device needs a CDSCO registration where it is a medical device. A 'miracle cure' that delays a proven treatment can cause harm.
33-6.cost: No cost to ask for the evidence. A second opinion from a government hospital is cheap.
33-6.caveats: Rehabilitation, physiotherapy and assistive devices can improve function; they are not a cure. A claim based only on testimonials is not evidence. Do not stop a proven treatment for a miracle cure.
33-6.sources: Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>; Consumer Protection Act, 2019. <https://consumeraffairs.nic.in/>; National Medical Commission. <https://www.nmc.org.in/>; Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation. <https://cdsco.gov.in/>

33-10.title: Mention your disability certificate in a job application: it can bring a reservation, a concession or a support
33-10.inPlainWords: A disability certificate and a UDID can make you eligible for a reservation in a government post, a fee concession, a scholarship and a workplace accommodation. Mention it at the application stage, not only at the interview, and keep a copy of the certificate. A private employer may also get a benefit for employing a person with a disability. You do not have to disclose a disability that does not affect the job, but a support or a reservation usually needs the certificate.
33-10.benefit: The RPwD Act, 2016 provides a 4% reservation in government establishments for the identified disabilities and requires an equal-opportunity policy. The UDID card is the single document for the benefits. A private employer can claim a deduction under the Income-tax Act for employing a person with a disability. The Act prohibits discrimination in promotion and pay. A reasonable accommodation can include a ramp, a screen reader or flexible hours.
33-10.cost: The certificate is free or low cost. A private employer's support varies.
33-10.caveats: A reservation applies to an identified post and a government establishment. A private employer is not bound by the 4% quota, but is bound by the anti-discrimination provisions. Keep the medical records for a reassessment.
33-10.sources: Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>; Department of Empowerment of Persons with Disabilities. <https://depwd.gov.in/>; Income-tax Department. <https://www.incometax.gov.in/>

33-20.title: If you are denied a job, a promotion or equal pay because of a disability, the RPwD Act gives you a remedy
33-20.inPlainWords: The Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016 prohibits discrimination in employment, promotion and pay, and requires a reasonable accommodation. A government establishment must follow the reservation and the equal-opportunity policy. A private employer must not discriminate. You can complain to the state commissioner for persons with disabilities, the labour authority or a court. Keep the advertisement, the emails and the pay records.
33-20.benefit: Sections 20 and 21 of the RPwD Act, 2016 prohibit discrimination and require an equal-opportunity policy. The state commissioner can inquire into a complaint and recommend action. The labour court or the civil court can award compensation. The Act also provides for a grievance redressal officer in a government establishment. A union or an NGO can help with the complaint.
33-20.cost: No cost to complain to the commissioner. A lawyer's fee for a court case; legal aid is available.
33-20.caveats: A 'disability' must fall within the Act's list and be certified. A delay can weaken the case. A settlement should be in writing.
33-20.sources: Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>; Department of Empowerment of Persons with Disabilities. <https://depwd.gov.in/>; National Legal Services Authority. <https://nalsa.gov.in/>

33-3.title: A psychiatric admission in India does not need a guardian to sign: the Mental Healthcare Act uses a nominated representative and a review board
33-3.cost: Government psychiatric hospitals and district hospitals charge nothing or a token amount, and the Act gives a right to affordable care. A private psychiatric hospital charges its own daily rate, which varies widely by city and by whether the ward is general or single-occupancy.
33-3.inPlainWords: If a person with a mental illness has the capacity to consent, they are admitted as a voluntary patient and can leave when they choose. If they lack that capacity, the Mental Healthcare Act, 2017 allows a supported admission of up to 30 days on the application of the person's nominated representative, but only after independent psychiatric and mental health assessments certify that admission is necessary. Nobody has to sign as a guardian. The capacity review the Act requires follows seven days after a supported admission where the nominated representative consented under section 89(7), and the Mental Health Review Board must review the admission. An advance directive and a nominated representative can be put in place in advance, while the person is well.
33-3.benefit: The Act gives every person the right to free or affordable mental health care from the state, and it makes the nominated representative the person who is consulted, not a guardian who decides. Sections 4 and 5 deal with capacity and the advance directive, section 14 with the nominated representative, section 89 with a supported admission that lasts up to 30 days, section 90 with a longer admission of 30 to 90 days that needs the Board's approval, and sections 73 to 82 with the Mental Health Review Board. Section 88 lets a voluntary patient be discharged, and section 89(3) says a supported patient must no longer remain in the establishment once the grounds for admission have ended.
33-3.sources: India Code, Mental Healthcare Act, 2017 (Act 10 of 2017). <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>; Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, mental health programmes. <https://mohfw.gov.in/>; National Legal Services Authority, legal aid for persons with mental illness. <https://nalsa.gov.in/>
33-3.caveats: If the person lacks capacity and has not named a nominated representative, the hospital has to follow the Act's procedure for that case, and a relative cannot simply admit them as a guardian. Keep the admission papers, the independent psychiatric and mental health assessments, and the Board reference number. If the person asks to leave and is not discharged, or the capacity review under section 89(8) of a supported admission does not happen, complain to the hospital's medical superintendent, then to the State Mental Health Authority and the Review Board. An emergency can justify a short admission while the paperwork is completed, but it still has to be reported and reviewed.

33-7.title: The one card that unlocks most Indian disability benefits is the UDID; the pension itself is paid by your state
33-7.inPlainWords: The Unique Disability ID card, or UDID, is the certificate most Indian disability schemes ask for. You apply on swavlambancard.gov.in, choose a government hospital, and a medical board assesses your disability; the card is then issued with a percentage and a disability code. With it you can apply for the state disability pension or allowance, the ADIP scheme for devices, Niramaya insurance, the income-tax deductions under sections 80U and 80DD, the 4 per cent reservation in government posts, and free or concessional travel where your state offers it. No single office hands all of this over at once: the card is central, but the pension amount and the extra benefits are set by each state, so the district social welfare office or the state disability directorate is where you apply for those.
33-7.benefit: The portal lets you track the application, download a soft copy and correct an error. A benchmark disability of 40 per cent or more is what most schemes require, and a higher percentage unlocks more: for example the ADIP income-linked subsidy and the higher income-tax deduction depend on it. The state pension is usually claimed with the UDID, a bank account in the applicant's name, an income or residence certificate and a photograph, and many states pay a higher rate at 80 per cent or more. Because the card is a single national record, it also makes it easier to carry one document instead of a district certificate plus a hospital letter.
33-7.cost: The UDID application itself is free on the portal, though a state may charge a small fee for the assessment or the printed card. Applying for the pension is free. Anyone offering to get you a UDID quickly for a fee is selling you something the portal does for nothing.
33-7.caveats: The disability percentage on the card is what the medical board assessed, and it can be reviewed if the condition changes. A pension from one state usually stops when you move to another, because the scheme is state-funded, so tell the new district office before you move. The UDID does not replace every document: a railway concession and some scholarships ask for their own form or a specific certificate. Keep a scanned copy and note the UDID number, because you will need it repeatedly.
33-7.sources: Department of Empowerment of Persons with Disabilities, Unique Disability ID. <https://swavlambancard.gov.in/>; Department of Empowerment of Persons with Disabilities, UDID. <https://depwd.gov.in/en/unique-disability-id-udid/>; Department of Empowerment of Persons with Disabilities, schemes and services. <https://depwd.gov.in/en/schemes-and-services/>

33-8.title: For a child under six the Indian help is devices, insurance and early intervention, not a national therapy allowance
33-8.inPlainWords: India has no national cash benefit that pays for a young child's therapy. What does exist is a set of separate schemes. The ADIP scheme pays most of the cost of aids and appliances for a family below an income ceiling. Niramaya, run by the National Trust, is a low-cost insurance policy for autism, cerebral palsy, intellectual disability and multiple disabilities that reimburses therapy, hospitalisation and corrective surgery up to a fixed yearly limit. The DDRS scheme funds non-governmental organisations that run early intervention and day-care services, the cross-disability early intervention centres assess and start therapy, and a government hospital's physical medicine and rehabilitation department is the cheapest place to begin. Apply with the UDID.
33-8.benefit: ADIP pays 100 per cent of the cost of an aid if the family's monthly income is Rs 22,500 or less, and 50 per cent if it is between Rs 22,501 and Rs 30,000, up to Rs 15,000 for most aids once in three years, up to Rs 30,000 for a high-end prosthesis, and up to Rs 50,000 towards a motorised tricycle or wheelchair once in five years. Niramaya gives cover of Rs 1 lakh on a reimbursement basis, with no pre-insurance medical test, at any hospital, for a person holding a UDID with one of the four National Trust disabilities. The DDRS grant reaches you through an NGO, so ask the district office which nearby organisation holds one.
33-8.cost: ADIP is free or half price according to the income slab, and the device has to be bought through an implementing agency or the PMD-VK and ARJUN portals. Niramaya charges a small annual premium set by the National Trust, so check the current rate on its site rather than relying on an old figure. Government hospital therapy is charged at the hospital's own nominal rates.
33-8.caveats: ADIP covers a given device once in three years, or once in five years for a motorised wheelchair, so plan the purchase and keep the receipt. Niramaya pays after you spend, so keep every prescription, bill and discharge summary, and remember that it is not a substitute for a health insurance policy. The income ceiling is the family's, and a household just above it pays the full market price. Private therapy is not covered by any national scheme, and the quality and cost of therapists vary widely.
33-8.sources: Department of Empowerment of Persons with Disabilities, ADIP scheme. <https://depwd.gov.in/en/adip-scheme/>; National Trust, Niramaya health insurance. <https://nationaltrust.nic.in/about-niramaya/>; Department of Empowerment of Persons with Disabilities, DDRS. <https://depwd.gov.in/en/ddrs/>; Department of Empowerment of Persons with Disabilities, cross-disability early intervention centres. <https://depwd.gov.in/en/cross-disability-early-intervention-centres/>

33-9.title: No national subsidy pays to adapt a private home; some states and municipal bodies do, and the rest is your own cost
33-9.inPlainWords: India has no central scheme that pays to widen a doorway, build a ramp or convert a bathroom in a private house. The accessibility duties in the Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016 fall on public buildings, transport, information and services, not on your landlord and not on your own home. What you can use: some states and municipal corporations run small grants or distribute ramps, grab rails and commode chairs through the district disability office; the ADIP scheme funds devices rather than construction; and a request to a landlord for a ramp is a reasonable request, though the Act does not force a private landlord to pay for it.
33-9.benefit: The practical route is a written application to the district social welfare officer or the state disability directorate asking whether a home-modification or independent-living grant exists in your state, with the UDID, income proof, a photograph of the entrance and a quotation from a contractor. Some municipal corporations attach a disability cell to their building-permission department, which can advise on a ramp that does not need approval. Where no grant exists, the cheapest changes are usually a portable ramp, a raised toilet seat and grab rails, and those are the items ADIP is most likely to fund.
33-9.cost: Where a state grant exists it is small and capped, and it may be paid only after the work is finished and inspected. Otherwise the whole cost is yours, and a contractor's quotation is the only reliable figure.
33-9.caveats: Do not pay anyone who promises a central home-modification subsidy: there is no such scheme. A landlord's refusal to build a ramp is not automatically unlawful, because the Act's accessibility duties do not bind a private dwelling. Put a request to a landlord in writing, keep the reply, and consider a portable ramp that you can take with you. If you rent a flat in a building with a residents' association, the association's approval is a separate step from the landlord's.
33-9.sources: Department of Empowerment of Persons with Disabilities, schemes and services. <https://depwd.gov.in/en/schemes-and-services/>; Department of Empowerment of Persons with Disabilities, ADIP scheme. <https://depwd.gov.in/en/adip-scheme/>; Department of Empowerment of Persons with Disabilities, the RPwD Act, 2016 and its rules. <https://depwd.gov.in/en/rpwd-act-2016/>

33-11.title: The income-tax deduction for your own disability is section 80U; for a dependant it is section 80DD
33-11.cost: The certificate is issued by a government hospital's medical board and is free or charged at the hospital's nominal rate. A tax preparer's fee is optional, and the portal walks you through the claim.
33-11.inPlainWords: If you have a disability of 40 per cent or more, section 80U lets you deduct Rs 75,000 from your taxable income, and if the disability is 80 per cent or more the deduction is Rs 1,25,000. If you support a dependant with a disability, section 80DD gives the same two amounts, and the money does not have to be spent on treatment: it can go towards their care, nursing or a trained attendant. You claim it in your income-tax return with a certificate from a government medical authority. There is no office to visit and no application to a tax officer, and no agent needs to be paid to get it.
33-11.benefit: The deduction is a flat amount, so it does not depend on how much you actually spent, and it is available every year that the disability continues. Section 80U is claimed by the person with the disability; section 80DD is claimed by the relative who supports them, and the dependant must be wholly or mainly dependent on that person. Only one of the two can be used for the same person in a year, so a family where the person with a disability has their own taxable income should decide which claim saves more. A severe disability at 80 per cent or more gives the higher figure under both sections.
33-11.sources: Income Tax Department, e-filing portal. <https://www.incometax.gov.in/iec/foportal/>; Income Tax Department, deductions for disability. <https://www.incometaxindia.gov.in/>; Department of Empowerment of Persons with Disabilities, UDID. <https://depwd.gov.in/en/unique-disability-id-udid/>
33-11.caveats: This is a deduction, not a payment: it reduces taxable income, so the saving is your marginal tax rate multiplied by the amount. If you file under the new regime in section 115BAC, most deductions of this kind are withdrawn, so work out both regimes before choosing, because for a family with a large medical bill the old regime can still be better. A certificate must be renewed if the disability changes, and a false certificate is an offence. Keep the certificate and the acknowledgement with your return papers.

33-12.title: Buses have to be accessible under the RPwD Act, but free travel is a state concession, not a national right
33-12.inPlainWords: The Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016 requires public transport to be made accessible, and it obliges the government to provide transport for a child with a disability and an attendant to reach school. What it does not do is make bus travel free everywhere. Free or concessional travel is decided by each state and each city transport undertaking: some cities have long allowed free travel for people with disabilities on their buses, others give a concession, and some give nothing. Ask the transport undertaking in your city what it offers and which document it wants, and ask the state disability department whether a bus pass scheme exists.
33-12.benefit: Sections 40 to 46 of the Act deal with accessibility of the built environment, transport, information and communication, and consumer goods, and the Accessible India Campaign audits and retrofits public transport and railway stations. Where a pass exists it is usually issued against the UDID or a disability certificate at a depot or online, and it may cover a companion as well. If a conductor refuses a valid concession, or a driver passes a wheelchair user by, that is a complaint to the transport undertaking and to the state commissioner for persons with disabilities, not something you have to argue on the footboard.
33-12.cost: Free where your city or state funds the concession; otherwise the ordinary fare, or a discounted pass at the rate the undertaking sets. The pass itself is usually free or nominal.
33-12.caveats: There is no statutory right to free travel across India, so a refusal in a city without a scheme is not necessarily unlawful. Assistance dogs are a gap: Indian law does not give a trained service dog a general right of entry the way some countries do, so ask the operator in advance and expect to negotiate. Accessible buses are unevenly rolled out, and a low-floor bus is not the same as an accessible stop. For a complaint, keep the bus number, the time and the route.
33-12.sources: Department of Empowerment of Persons with Disabilities, the RPwD Act, 2016 and its rules. <https://depwd.gov.in/en/rpwd-act-2016/>; Department of Empowerment of Persons with Disabilities, schemes and services. <https://depwd.gov.in/en/schemes-and-services/>; Ministry of Road Transport and Highways. <https://morth.gov.in/>

33-13.title: Exam boards must give accommodation, but you have to ask with your certificate before the form closes
33-13.inPlainWords: Indian exam bodies publish a list of facilities for candidates with disabilities: a scribe, extra time, a separate room, a magnifier, an assistive device, and in some exams a choice of centre. You get them by declaring the disability and uploading the certificate when you apply, not by asking the invigilator on the day. The Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act requires educational institutions to provide the support, and the Central Board of Secondary Education, the National Testing Agency for CUET and NEET, and each state board publish their own rules and deadlines in the examination bulletin. Read the bulletin for your exam before the form closes.
33-13.benefit: The usual steps are: tick the disability option in the application, upload the UDID or the disability certificate, apply separately for a scribe where the exam allows one, and carry the admit card, the certificate and an identity document to the centre. If the centre cannot provide what was approved, ask for the centre superintendent and put the request in writing on the spot, then complain to the board or the testing agency afterwards with the acknowledgement. The state commissioner for persons with disabilities can take up a persistent refusal.
33-13.cost: The accommodation itself is free. A board or agency usually arranges the scribe, and where you bring your own, its eligibility rules apply.
33-13.caveats: Deadlines are strict and a request made after the correction window is normally refused, so diarise the date. The percentage of extra time and the list of permitted devices differ from exam to exam and change between years, so read the current bulletin rather than a senior's account. A scribe is usually required to be a student of a lower standard and not a relative. If a centre is physically inaccessible, ask for a change of centre when you apply, because it cannot be fixed on the day.
33-13.sources: Central Board of Secondary Education, academic and examination circulars. <https://cbseacademic.nic.in/>; National Testing Agency. <https://nta.ac.in/>; Department of Empowerment of Persons with Disabilities, the RPwD Act, 2016 and its rules. <https://depwd.gov.in/en/rpwd-act-2016/>

33-14.title: School is a right under the RTE Act and the RPwD Act; home-based education is the fallback, not the first choice
33-14.inPlainWords: The Right to Education Act gives every child aged six to fourteen free and compulsory education in a neighbourhood school, and the Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act adds that a school must admit a child with a disability without discrimination and provide the support the child needs. Where a child cannot attend even with that support, the law treats home-based education as an alternative that the state education department has to arrange, not something a parent has to organise alone. A school that refuses admission, charges a capitation fee, or pushes a child out because of the disability is breaking the law, and the remedy starts with a written complaint to the district education officer.
33-14.benefit: Section 16 of the RPwD Act lists the duties of an educational institution, including admitting a child without discrimination, providing the facilities the child needs, and arranging transport for the child and an attendant; section 17 sets out the measures for inclusive education. Under the RTE Act the neighbourhood school cannot charge a fee, and the 25 per cent entry-level quota in private schools is free to the parent. The Samagra Shiksha programme funds resource teachers, aids and ramps in government schools, so ask the block education officer what the school can claim.
33-14.cost: A government school is free, including textbooks, uniform and the mid-day meal. A private school's fee is its own, but a seat under the RTE quota costs the parent nothing.
33-14.caveats: Home-based education is meant for a child who cannot attend even with support, and the state has to arrange it; a school cannot use it to avoid admitting the child. Put a refusal in writing with the date and the name of the person who refused, because a complaint without a record is easy to deny. The RTE Act covers ages six to fourteen, so for an older child the RPwD Act and the state's scheme apply, and for a younger child the anganwadi and early intervention route. Expelling a child because of a disability is discrimination, not discipline.
33-14.sources: Department of Empowerment of Persons with Disabilities, the RPwD Act, 2016 and its rules. <https://depwd.gov.in/en/rpwd-act-2016/>; Ministry of Education. <https://www.education.gov.in/>; Central Board of Secondary Education, academic circulars. <https://cbseacademic.nic.in/>

33-15.title: India has no separate disability licence: you take the ordinary test at the RTO, with a medical certificate and an adapted car
33-15.inPlainWords: Unlike some countries, India does not issue a special category of driving licence for people with disabilities. You apply for an ordinary learner's licence and then a permanent licence at the regional transport office, and the medical certificate the RTO requires has to state that you are fit to drive, with any adaptation noted. A car fitted with hand controls, a left-foot accelerator or an automatic gearbox can be driven once the adaptation is recorded, and some offices ask you to take the test in that car. For a hearing impairment the office may ask for a specialist's opinion; for uncontrolled epilepsy or poor vision the fitness rules are stricter.
33-15.benefit: The application is made on the Parivahan portal or at the RTO, with Form 1 for the medical certificate and Form 1A where the office asks for it, photographs and address proof, and the learner's test is a short computer or oral test on road rules. A licence issued with an adaptation carries that condition, which is what an insurer and a traffic officer look for. The vehicle itself must be adapted by a workshop that will give you a written certificate of the work, and the insurance policy should record the adaptation so that a claim is not refused on the ground that the car was modified.
33-15.cost: The RTO fee is set by the state and is listed on the Parivahan portal; a driving school and an adaptation workshop charge separately, and the adaptation is the large item.
33-15.caveats: Practice varies between states and even between offices, so telephone the RTO before you go and ask which form it wants for your disability. A refusal has to be in writing, and it can be challenged before the transport commissioner. A licence is not a right to drive unsafely: if the condition changes, or a seizure happens, you have to stop and be reassessed. Do not let a driving school promise a licence without the medical step; that is how licences get cancelled later.
33-15.sources: Ministry of Road Transport and Highways, Parivahan Sewa. <https://parivahan.gov.in/parivahan/>; Ministry of Road Transport and Highways. <https://morth.gov.in/>; Department of Empowerment of Persons with Disabilities, the RPwD Act, 2016 and its rules. <https://depwd.gov.in/en/rpwd-act-2016/>

33-18.title: No court now declares an adult with a disability wholly incapable; Indian law uses support and limited guardianship
33-18.cost: A court application costs court fees and a lawyer's fee, and it takes months. The National Trust committee route is cheaper and faster but is limited to its four disabilities.
33-18.inPlainWords: The Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016 states that a person with a disability enjoys legal capacity on an equal basis with others, and it replaced the old model in which a court declared someone of unsound mind incapable and appointed a guardian over everything. Now a district court, or an authority the state government notifies, can appoint only a limited guardian: a joint arrangement for a specific decision and a specific period, made according to the person's own will, and only where the person has been given support and still cannot take a legally binding decision. Total support is exceptional and is reviewed. Section 14(2) also deems every guardian appointed under any other law to function as a limited guardian.
33-18.benefit: In practice the person keeps the right to decide about their money, property, treatment, marriage and vote, and a guardian's signature is not needed for ordinary decisions. Where a bank, a registrar or a hospital insists on a guardian, quote sections 13 and 14 and ask for the refusal in writing, then take it to the state commissioner for persons with disabilities. For the four disabilities covered by the National Trust Act, a local level committee can appoint a guardian under section 14 of that Act, which is a separate and usually quicker route for autism, cerebral palsy, intellectual disability and multiple disabilities.
33-18.sources: Department of Empowerment of Persons with Disabilities, the RPwD Act, 2016 and its rules. <https://depwd.gov.in/en/rpwd-act-2016/>; National Trust, legal guardianship. <https://nationaltrust.nic.in/about-legal-guardianship/>; India Code. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>
33-18.caveats: The Act does not abolish guardianship for children: a minor's property is still dealt with under the Guardians and Wards Act, 1890. A limited guardianship order can be reviewed and appealed, and it does not transfer the person's rights to the guardian. If a relative is managing someone's money without any order, that is a civil dispute about the money, not a legal guardianship, and it should be challenged rather than regularised. Keep the order, the period and the decisions it covers in writing.

33-19.title: A guardian in India is not automatically liable for harm an adult with a disability causes; that adult's own assets are answerable
33-19.inPlainWords: There is no Indian rule that makes a guardian pay for damage an adult with a disability causes, the way a parent answers for a young child. An adult is responsible for their own civil wrongs, and a court can order compensation out of that person's assets; a limited guardian appointed under the Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act decides jointly with the person on specified matters and does not become an insurer of their conduct. For a minor, the parents are liable. What actually protects a family is insurance and paperwork, not a guardian's promise: a personal accident policy, a householder's liability cover, and for a driver a motor policy that records any adaptation.
33-19.benefit: A limited guardian should keep the person's money separate, record what was spent and why, and keep the appointment order with the list of decisions it covers, because that record is what a court will look at if a dispute arises. If a claim is threatened, the person's own insurer conducts the defence and the guardian is not a party unless the guardian did something wrong. A guardian who takes money or neglects the person is personally liable for that, and can be removed by the court or authority that appointed them.
33-19.cost: Insurance premiums depend on the cover; legal aid through the district legal services authority is free for a person who qualifies, and NALSA's network can advise before a claim is filed.
33-19.caveats: This is a general account, not advice on a specific case: the facts decide, and a lawyer should see the papers. Do not sign an undertaking that you are responsible for all harm the person may cause, because no law requires it and a signed undertaking can be enforced as a contract. Guardianship is not a way to take over someone's property, and a transfer made by a limited guardian outside the order can be set aside. If a relative is already acting as a guardian without an order, regularise it or stop.
33-19.sources: Department of Empowerment of Persons with Disabilities, the RPwD Act, 2016 and its rules. <https://depwd.gov.in/en/rpwd-act-2016/>; National Legal Services Authority. <https://nalsa.gov.in/>; India Code. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>

33-4.title: For caregivers of disabled family members at home, it’s vital to watch your own health
33-4.cost: There’s no cost involved. Simply share some of the caregiving duties and use that time to get a medical checkup.
33-4.inPlainWords: It’s not exaggeration when caregivers feel completely exhausted. One U.S. study followed over 800 older adults for four years. Those caring for a disabled spouse while also reporting high levels of mental strain had a mortality risk roughly 63% higher than people who weren’t caregivers. No such increase appeared among caregivers who didn’t report feeling stressed. So the real issue isn’t caregiving itself, but the long-term strain it causes.
33-4.benefit: This prospective cohort study ran from 1993 to 1998, with an average follow-up period of 4.5 years across four U.S. communities. It included 392 caregivers and 427 non-caregivers aged 66–96 who all lived with their spouses. Over four years, 103 participants (12.6%) passed away. After adjusting for socioeconomic factors, pre-existing conditions, and subclinical cardiovascular disease, caregivers reporting mental or emotional stress had a 63% higher mortality risk compared to non-caregivers (RR 1.63, 95% CI 1.00–2.65). No significant increase in mortality was seen among caregivers without reported stress (RR 1.08, 95% CI 0.61–1.90) or among spouses who were disabled but not cared for by their partners (RR 1.37, 95% CI 0.73–2.58).
33-4.sources: Schulz R, Beach SR (1999). Caregiving as a risk factor for mortality: the Caregiver Health Effects Study. JAMA, 282(23):2215-2219. <https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.282.23.2215>
33-4.caveats: Caution: The lower bound of the confidence interval here is exactly 1.00, meaning there remains a small chance that no actual difference exists. This study focused on older U.S. adults living with disabled spouses, so its findings may not fully apply to caregivers of younger disabled family members. Still, it clearly shows that those experiencing high stress face greater risk. Whenever possible, share caregiving duties with others; contact local disability associations, or a District Disability Rehabilitation Centre, for respite care or day programmes. Caregivers should also keep taking any prescribed medications — see Section 16, Item 1. The main beneficiary of all this advice is you.

33-17.title: Getting a hearing aid when hearing declines — the reason is to hear better now, not to prevent dementia
33-17.cost: Hearing aids cost several thousand to tens of thousands of rupees; most must be paid for out of pocket. Fitting requires professional testing and multiple follow‑up adjustments.
33-17.inPlainWords: The claim that “wearing a hearing aid prevents dementia” currently lacks solid evidence. A three‑year trial involving nearly a thousand participants found no overall difference between groups. Only among people already at higher risk of cognitive decline did a modest benefit appear. Thus, the main reason to get a hearing aid is to hear clearly now — to talk with others and hear traffic while crossing the street — not to protect the brain decades later.
33-17.benefit: The ACHIEVE trial took place in four U.S. communities and enrolled 977 individuals aged 70–84 with untreated hearing loss but no obvious cognitive impairment. Participants were randomly assigned to either hearing intervention (counseling and hearing aid fitting) or health‑education control, with follow‑up every six months. The primary endpoint was change in overall cognitive scores over three years. In the combined analysis of both participant cohorts, there was no significant difference: the intervention group showed a change of −0.200 (95% CI −0.256 to −0.144) versus −0.202 (95% CI −0.258 to −0.145) in the control group; the difference was 0.002 (95% CI −0.077 to 0.081, P = 0.96). A pre‑specified sensitivity analysis revealed a statistically significant interaction (P = 0.010) between the two cohorts. The second cohort comprised older participants with more risk factors for cognitive decline and lower baseline cognitive scores. Researchers concluded that hearing intervention may modestly slow cognitive decline over three years in high‑risk individuals but not in those at lower risk. No serious adverse events attributable to the intervention were reported.
33-17.sources: Lin FR, Pike JR, Albert MS, et al.; ACHIEVE Collaborative Research Group (2023). Hearing intervention versus health education control to reduce cognitive decline in older adults with hearing loss in the USA (ACHIEVE): a multicentre, randomised controlled trial. Lancet, 402(10404):786-797. <https://doi.org/10.1016/S0140-6736(23)01406-X>
33-17.caveats: Controversy: The oft‑quoted claim that “hearing aids cut cognitive decline by nearly half” stems from a subgroup analysis of this trial, not its primary result, which showed no overall difference. This note is included to separate the practical benefit of hearing aids from the unproven dementia‑prevention claim. Exam bodies and universities have to provide reasonable accommodations under the Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016; see item 13 in this section. A driver with hearing loss should wear the hearing aids the licensing authority expects; see item 15 in this section.
